title: Inquest into Sault man's death gives family 'closure'
subtitle: Jury recommends defibrillators in police cruisers after 2016 death of John Roberts
article: A jury has recommended that the Ontario Association of Chiefs of Police and the province examine the feasibility of equipping all police vehicles with portable defibrillators.
The recommendation came at the end of a two-day inquest into the Dec. 15, 2016, death of John Roberts, 49, of Sault Ste. Marie.

Roberts had been arrested following an impaired driving complaint on Highway 17 near Bonfield shortly before 3 p.m. He was pronounced dead at the North Bay Regional Health Centre at 4:15 p.m. that day.
The five-member coroner's jury ruled that Roberts died of acute fentanyl and cocaine intoxication, combined with an underlying heart disease.
The inquest was convened to answer the who, how, when, where and by what means Roberts died and whether the manner of death was natural, accidental, suicide, homicide or undetermined.
An inquest is mandatory in deaths which occur while a person is in custody or being detained.
Jurors may make recommendations based on the evidence presented to them, however they are not required to make recommendations.
The jury is also prohibited from making any finding of legal responsibility or expressing any conclusion of law.
"This was more or less about closure," Roberts's daughter, Alexis Roberts, of Sault Ste. Marie, said following the verdict.
"We didn't have any closure before this."
Alexis Roberts, who attended both days of the inquest with her grandmother, said she was satisfied with the jury finding and recommendation.
The inquest before Dr. Steven Bodley and a five-member jury heard from two witnesses Tuesday, including the forensic pathologist who performed the autopsy on Roberts the day after his death.
Dr. Martin Queen said the amount of fentanyl in Roberts' body could in itself have been sufficient to cause his death following his arrest.
But Roberts also had cocaine in his system and had sometime in the past - possibly years earlier - suffered heart damage.
"Some time ago, probably a number of years, he suffered a complete blockage" of the coronary artery, Queen said.
And although Roberts recovered from the heart attack, his heart had been damaged and would never return to normal.
That damage, he said, increased the risk of future heart troubles.
But unlike a TV show, he said, it is impossible to determine how much each of those factors played in Roberts' death.
"If it was only the fentanyl" in his system, Queen testified, "it would have been a slam dunk" to determine the cause of death.
But Roberts also had cocaine in his system, and that, combined with damage to his heart, made determining the cause of Roberts' death more complicated.
"I can't assign a percentage to the factors," Queen said.
He noted that the amount of fentanyl in Roberts' body was "quite high," but he had no idea what his level of tolerance to the drug was.
"It definitely could have killed him," Queen said.
But there is also the possibility the combination of cocaine and the pre-existing heart damage could have killed him.
Roberts was stopped by OPP Sgt. Brent Turner at about 2:45 p.m. on Highway 17 near Highway 531 after a member of the public had reported an erratic driver westbound on Highway 17.
Roberts went into medical distress shortly after he was stopped.
Turner drove with lights flashing and siren sounding to meet an ambulance near Corbeil Corners, where Turner and another OPP officer performed CPR on Roberts at the side of the road.
Roberts was transferred to the ambulance and taken to the North Bay Regional Health Centre.
He was pronounced dead at 4:15 p.m.

Queen said that during his examination of Roberts' body, he found no external injuries. But during the internal examination, he found Roberts' heard showed sign of "significant heart disease. His heart was a bit heavier than normal" and there was damage to the heart muscle that was not recent.
His lungs were also "remarkably heavy" with fluid in them. The lungs, he said, were three to four times heavier than normal weight.
He said an overdose of certain drugs, specifically opioids such as fentanyl, can cause fluid build-up in the lungs similar to what he found.

In earlier testimony, Dr. Nathalie Desrosiers of the Centre for Forensic Sciences, said testing of blood provided following the autopsy showed a concentration of 25 nanograms of fentanyl per millilitre of blood, but only trace amounts of cocaine.
Desrosiers said the concentration of fentanyl in the blood "could be the cause of death," and was at the "higher end" of fentanyl concentration.
She said cocaine "degrades fairly quickly compared to other drugs."
Queen agreed, saying that "just because it's a trace amount doesn't mean it is irrelevant to the death."

He said many drugs remain "quite stable in the body," but cocaine immediately starts to degrade. Even over the 16-and-a-half hours between Roberts' death and the start of the autopsy the next morning, the level of cocaine in his body would continue to degrade. In fact, he said, it will continue to degrade when it is placed in the tubes for shipment to the Centre for Forensic Sciences, right up until the time it is tested.
Queen also explained that while the body will build up a tolerance to opiates, "cocaine is not like that. A person can be killed by a relatively low dose even for regular users."
In fact, he said, people who take cocaine over a period of time actually become more susceptible to dying of a cocaine overdose.

To someone with an underlying heart disease, Queen said, taking cocaine increases the risk. It makes the heart pump harder and faster and increases the blood pressure, putting more strain on the heart.
In his charge to the jury, Bodley said their role was to answer five questions - who died, how that person died, when that person died, where that person died and by what manner the person died.
The jury could decide the person died of natural causes, by accident, by suicide, by homicide or of undetermined cause.
